title: The Important Peculiarities of Memory
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Working from Bjork and Bjork's account of memory's "important peculiarities", Hendrick sets out four properties of human memory that he argues should govern how teachers plan. Storage capacity is vast while retrieval is fallible, which is why spacing and retrieval practice matter and why students routinely believe they know material they cannot recall. What can be retrieved depends on environmental, interpersonal, emotional and bodily cues, a finding he turns against activity-heavy lessons: a crime-scene investigation or Shakespeare rewritten as text messages may be memorable as an experience while leaving the intended content unlearned. Retrieval itself alters the memory, Bartlett's schema insight a century ago, which makes recall untrustworthy but also strengthens future access. Finally, older representations become more accessible over time while recent ones fade, explaining why times tables survive when yesterday's lesson does not. The practical conclusion Hendrick draws is that retrieval should be treated as a learning event rather than a test, since material is learned across episodes distributed in time rather than at the moment of first encounter.
points: Hendrick's headline inference from fallible retrieval is that students' confidence in their own knowledge is systematically unreliable, which is the case for spacing and retrieval practice rather than re-reading.
The cue-dependence of recall is used to puncture the assumption that novel or dramatic lessons are memorable ones, with students experiencing the activity rather than learning the content.
He notes in passing that hunger diminishes learning and cites PISA data putting UK pupils missing a weekly meal at 11 per cent against an OECD average of 8.
Treating retrieval as reconstruction rather than playback explains both why memory is untrustworthy and why successful recall strengthens later access to the same material.
The reframing of retrieval as a learning event rather than an assessment is the piece's operational takeaway for curriculum and review design.
quotes: One of the most important things educators need to know about learning is that human memory is not like a tape recorder or a computer. It has what Bjork and Bjork call “important peculiarities”, four of which are really important to know when planning teaching.

In other words, while we can store a wealth of information, the mechanisms for recalling that information are imperfect and prone to error. We often think we know something when we don't really know it at all.

So lessons where there are a lot of activities/props etc. such as students doing a crime scene investigation or rewriting Shakespeare in text messages, lessons which are usually thought of as 'memorable' may not actually be memorable at all - it may seem like learning is happening but actually students are probably experiencing something rather than learning it.
The important point here is that successfully retrieving a memory can strengthen its future recovery, making future retrievals easier.

The key takeaway here is that we should view retrieval as a learning event. Retrieval practice is not so much about testing whether someone knows something but rather a core part of actually learning that something, a process which occurs across time and space.
When we 'learn' something by reading it or being taught it, we don't learn it in that moment, we learn it across a number of episodes yet to happen in the future.

Ultimately, educators should be aware that memory is a highly dynamic process in which memories are not recalled like a tape recorder or from a computer hard-drive but rather reshaped and consolidated according to how we access them.
